title: Clinic Scheduling Software for Residency Programs
description: Scheduling Wizard vs QGenda, Amion, Lightning Bolt and general clinic tools: which clinic scheduling software actually fits residency and fellowship programs.
content:
A note before the list: we are Scheduling Wizard. We build physician schedules as a service, so we have included ourselves below and you should read our entry with that in mind. General clinic tools come first as context. In the residency list that follows, the order is by one thing only, who actually builds the schedule, which is why a service comes first and the spreadsheet second; the software and the platforms you publish through follow. Rank by cost, or by how good the mobile app is, and the order changes. We have described the other tools as their own users and documentation describe them.

Summary

  • Graduate Medical Education (GME) scheduling is a rules problem that general booking software is not built for, so many programs still run it in spreadsheets that reset every July.
  • GME-specific software exists, but self-service tools still require chief residents to learn the platform and bear the administrative burden of schedule creation.
  • Managed scheduling services take this burden by delivering finished schedules built to the ACGME requirements the program says apply, with no software for the program to learn or operate.
  • To solve the annual scheduling scramble and preserve institutional knowledge, programs can use a managed service like Scheduling Wizard to receive complete schedules.

It's July 1st. The new chief resident opens a cryptic handover spreadsheet, FINAL_schedule_v12_USE_THIS_ONE.xlsx, and the annual continuity crisis officially begins. This scene plays out in teaching hospitals across the country, forcing each new chief to rebuild institutional scheduling knowledge from scratch.

Most clinic scheduling software was not built for Graduate Medical Education (GME). It was built for appointment booking or enterprise workforce management, not for the interlocking residency rotations, call schedules and ACGME rules a program has to hold together.

This guide evaluates the top clinic scheduling software for GME, separating general-purpose tools from GME-specific solutions.

Why GME Scheduling Is Different

Residency scheduling is a rules problem, not just a calendar-filling task. Dozens of variables intersect simultaneously. You can't write a call schedule without knowing the block/rotation schedule, and you can't finalize the block schedule without accounting for clinic assignments. Every decision ripples through ACGME duty hour limits, resident vacation requests, and conference obligations.

Appointment booking software is not built around this interdependence. It has no notion of a post-call day or of 80 hours a week averaged over four weeks. Nor is it designed to build block, call and clinic together, which is where fairness is won or lost. As one Reddit thread captured, residents want scheduling decided by rules, "not favoritism or bias at all."

This is the crux of why residency programs need to evaluate GME-specific options separately, and why we've organized this review into two distinct tiers.

Tier 1: General Clinic Scheduling Software

These tools are built for patient booking and staff coordination rather than for GME rotations.

Good for Appointments, Not for Rotations

This type of clinic scheduling software is widely used in healthcare settings for patient booking and staff coordination. They're polished, well-supported, and useful, just not for the multi-layered complexity of a residency program.

Acuity Scheduling

Acuity is an appointment scheduling tool owned by Squarespace. It handles client self-scheduling 24/7, customizable intake forms, automated reminders to reduce no-shows, and integrations with Google Calendar, Stripe, and Zoom.

The GME Gap

Acuity is not built for block rotations, call schedules or ACGME work hour rules. It's built to fill appointment slots, not to build a year-long, compliant, and equitable rotation schedule for a cohort of residents. If your program needs to manage patient-facing appointment booking at a clinic, Acuity is a solid pick. For scheduling residents, it is not the right fit.

WellSky

WellSky is a clinical operations platform used primarily in multi-location practices and post-acute care settings. It integrates scheduling with patient management workflows and offers strong reporting features for care coordination.

The GME Gap

WellSky is built for clinical operations, not graduate medical education. It doesn't account for the educational and regulatory framework that governs residency programs. It is not designed for rotation management, ACGME work hour tracking or the interplay between call, clinic and block schedules.

Skedulo

Skedulo is a workforce scheduling platform originally designed for mobile, field-based workers. It uses intelligent scheduling logic to dispatch workers to jobs and has customers in parts of healthcare such as home and community care.

The GME Gap

Skedulo is built for assignment-to-job matching, not for building a complex, multi-month schedule that governs an entire cohort of physicians-in-training. It is not set up around training levels or subspecialty ACGME rules.

Where Tier 1 Tools Fit

These tools are excellent in their intended contexts. But if your goal is building a compliant, fair, and sustainable residency or fellowship schedule, you will likely end up back in a spreadsheet.

Tier 2: Options Residency Programs Actually Use

These are the options residency and fellowship programs actually weigh.

Built for Residency, Fellowship, and High-Stakes Compliance

They range from a service to a spreadsheet to software built with GME in mind. Evaluate these if your program is serious about ending the annual scheduling scramble.

1. Scheduling Wizard

The only managed service on this list. No software to learn; finished schedules delivered as Excel, Google Sheets or a custom live view.

Scheduling Wizard is a done-for-you managed scheduling service with no software to learn. Programs submit their rules, requests and resident preferences, and our team delivers the finished block, clinic, call and attending schedules as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you, built to the ACGME requirements you tell us apply. There is no platform to log into, and the rules stay written down when the chief rotates out.

Best For

Programs that want the administrative burden of schedule creation taken off their plate, not just part of it handled.

How It Works

You share your program's rules (duty hours, rotation requirements, subspecialty rules, vacation requests, conference schedules). Our team works across all of it and returns a finished schedule. That schedule can be uploaded into your existing publishing platform or a shared hospital calendar, or you can use our live view, or both.

Key Strengths

  • The ACGME requirements built in, not just flagged after the fact. The subspecialty requirements you tell us apply are built into the schedule itself.
  • Minimal operator burden, as the scheduling knowledge lives with the service, not with whichever chief resident happens to be on duty this year.
  • Complete schedules for Block/Rotation, Call, Clinic, and Attending, not just one or two.
  • Fair call distribution, as we spread night shifts, weekends, and post-clinic assignments across the cohort, addressing one of the most common sources of resident dissatisfaction.
  • The platform is your choice. Many programs use Amion or QGenda for day-to-day schedule viewing. You can upload our schedules into it, use our live view, or both; it is entirely up to you.

Pricing

Contact Scheduling Wizard for a quote. Pricing is based on program size and complexity. The service currently supports 20+ hospitals and practices and 30+ departments and is backed by Y Combinator (YC W26).

What you get: finished schedules in Excel or Google Sheets, plus a custom live view if your program wants one. Mid-year redrafts are part of it. Clinic grids are the ones that move most, and rebuilding around a change is our job rather than something you pay extra for or do yourself. For the specifics, see our page on residency scheduling software.

2. Excel / Google Sheets

The clinic grid in most programs started life in a spreadsheet, and often still lives in one. It ranks second because nothing else matches it for flexibility: continuity panels, half-day splits, a resident who needs Thursdays protected for a research block. You type it and it is done.

The limits show up where clinic meets everything else. Clinic assignments have to agree with the block schedule, the call schedule and conference. Change one and three others move. A spreadsheet will not tell you which three. It also does not retain why last year's grid looked the way it did, which is the part a program feels every July.

3. QGenda

QGenda is an enterprise physician scheduling and workforce management platform. It includes GME-specific modules and offers broad visibility across departments and specialties.

Best For

Large health systems with dedicated scheduling coordinators and IT resources to manage the platform.

Key Strengths

Multi-department visibility, some ACGME compliance flagging, strong reporting, and integration with major EHR systems.

Drawbacks

For a single residency program, it is worth weighing the setup against who will run it. It is a self-service platform, meaning the administrative burden still falls on your chief resident or program coordinator. Some programs keep QGenda for viewing and distribution and have us build the schedule that goes into it.

4. Amion

Amion is a familiar name in residency scheduling. Most programs use it to publish and share schedules rather than to build them.

Best For

Publishing and sharing a finished on-call schedule with your team. Simple, and familiar to most residents.

Key Strengths

Clean, mobile-accessible interface. Most residents already know how to use it.

Drawbacks

Amion is built to publish and share the schedule; generation and compliance belong to whatever creates it. In that workflow the schedule is built before it goes into Amion, and the building usually falls to the chief resident. This is why many programs use Amion as a front-end publishing platform while relying on a separate service or tool to build the schedule.

5. Lightning Bolt (PerfectServe)

Lightning Bolt, now part of PerfectServe, generates shift-based schedules from rules you configure. It's particularly well-suited to specialties with clear shift structures, such as Emergency Medicine.

Best For

Shift-heavy programs where schedule generation can be templated and automated with relatively clear rules.

Key Strengths

Automated shift generation, real-time schedule updates, mobile access, and some capacity for handling complex call patterns.

Drawbacks

ACGME compliance support requires user verification. Setup and configuration place a meaningful burden on the chief resident or coordinator. For programs with complex, multi-layered rotation structures, the generated draft may still need adjusting by hand.

Planning for the Next July 1st

The annual scheduling scramble has been normalized in GME, but it shouldn't be. Every year, a new chief resident inherits an incomprehensible spreadsheet, spends weeks decoding it, and then spends the rest of their chief year buried in administrative work that has nothing to do with becoming a better physician. As one chief put it in a Reddit thread on scheduling tools, the entire system feels designed to make scheduling as painful as possible.

For programs that want to not just improve their GME scheduling software but escape the burden entirely, a managed service is the most direct path. Scheduling Wizard keeps your rules written down across chief rotations, builds in the ACGME requirements you tell us apply, and balances call to written rules, which takes much of the politics out of fairness.

Your residents didn't match into a residency to spend their nights building Excel formulas. Give them a service that handles the complexity so they can focus on what actually matters: learning medicine and caring for patients.

Frequently Asked Questions

How does Scheduling Wizard work with the platform we already use?

It is entirely up to you. We build the schedule either way, and deliver it in the format and structure you want: Excel or Google Sheets, or a custom live view we build for you if that is useful. Many programs keep the platform they already have for day-to-day viewing and upload our schedules straight into it; others use the live view, or both. Whatever works best for your program.

How do you handle ACGME compliance for my specific subspecialty?

You tell us which requirements apply to your program, the Common Program Requirements and anything your specialty's Review Committee adds, and we write them down with you alongside your own rules before the first build. They go into the schedule while it is built rather than being flagged afterwards. We do not assume we know your requirements better than you do; we ask.

What is the difference between a managed scheduling service and scheduling software?

A managed scheduling service, like Scheduling Wizard, builds the entire schedule for you, while scheduling software is a tool you must learn and operate yourself. With a managed service, you provide your program's rules and requests, and we deliver a finished schedule. With software (like QGenda), your chief resident or coordinator is still responsible for learning the platform, inputting all data, and manually resolving scheduling conflicts. A service takes this administrative burden off the program.

Why is GME scheduling so much harder than other types of staff scheduling?

GME scheduling is a rules problem, not just a task of filling calendar slots. It requires balancing dozens of interdependent variables simultaneously: ACGME duty hour rules, block rotation assignments, call duties, clinic schedules, individual vacation requests, and educational requirements. A change in one area has a cascading effect on all others, which is why generic scheduling tools are not suitable for the task.

Can private physician practices use Scheduling Wizard?

Yes, while our core focus is on GME programs, we also build for private practices and provider groups. We build fair schedules for attending physicians, NPs, and PAs, helping reduce administrative work for practice managers and promoting equitable distribution of call, clinic, and vacation time.

How much does Scheduling Wizard cost?

Pricing for our GME scheduling service is based on the size of your program and the complexity of your scheduling rules. This fee covers the complete creation of your Block, Call, Clinic, and Attending schedules for the entire academic year. It covers redrafts through the year, and the rules stay with us from one chief to the next.
